slots.label: ordinary-sale misconception
slots.description: Short selling means selling shares you already own because you expect a decline.
slots.repair: Selling owned shares exits a long position; short selling creates an obligation because borrowed shares must be returned.
slots.repairQuestion: What makes a short sale different from simply selling stock you already own?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner mentions borrowed shares or the later duty to return equivalent shares.

slots.label: risk-capped misconception
slots.description: Short selling can only lose the amount originally received from selling the shares.
slots.repair: The buyback price can exceed the sale price by a lot, so losses can exceed the original proceeds.
slots.repairQuestion: If shares are sold short at $80 and later cost $200 to buy back, what happens?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner says the short seller loses money because covering costs more than the sale proceeds.

slots.label: illegal-manipulation misconception
slots.description: All short selling is illegal market manipulation.
slots.repair: Ordinary short selling is regulated and can be used for speculation, hedging, or liquidity. Manipulative conduct such as spreading false rumors is a separate problem.
slots.repairQuestion: How is a regulated short sale different from manipulative short-and-distort behavior?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner distinguishes ordinary regulated borrowing/selling from illegal manipulation or false rumors.

slots.text: Short selling reverses the usual buy-then-sell order: borrow shares, sell them, then buy replacement shares to return. Falling prices can create profit; rising prices create losses and margin pressure. Ordinary short selling is regulated and distinct from manipulative rumor-driven trading.
